a: son of Elkiah son of Elihu son of Hilkiah
p: Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus, followed by the KJV, add four generations between Elkiah and Elihu.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: υἱοῦ Ἑλκειὰ υἱοῦ Ἠλειοὺ υἱοῦ Χελκείου
readings.en: son of Elkia, son of Eliu, son of Chelkias
readings.plain: son of Elkiah son of Elihu son of Hilkiah

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), in Swete's notes (Swete's line breaks removed)
readings.orig: +υιου Ανανιου υιου Γεδεων υιου Ραφαειν υιου Αχιτωβ ℵ
readings.en: adds after Elkia: son of Ananias, son of Gedeon, son of Raphaein, son of Achitob
readings.plain: son of Elkiah son of Ananias son of Gideon son of Raphain son of Ahitub son of Elihu son of Hilkiah

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), in Swete's notes; KJV
readings.orig: + υιου Ανανιου· υιου Γεδεων· υιου Ραφαιν· υιου Ακιθω·) A … om υιου Χελκειου A
readings.en: adds the same four names (Akitho for Achitob) and omits "son of Chelkias"
readings.plain: son of Elkiah son of Ananias son of Gideon son of Raphain son of Akitho son of Elihu

why: The Plain English Translation follows Vaticanus. The added names may have been lost from B by a scribe's eye skipping from one "son of" to another, or added later to lengthen the line; there is no way to be sure. The KJV follows the longer form, without Hilkiah, as in Alexandrinus.

a: the days before the new moons and the new moons
p: Vaticanus lists only the eves of the new moons; Sinaiticus and a corrector of Vaticanus add the new moons themselves.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), in Swete's notes; a corrector of Vaticanus in the margin (Bᵃᵇ); KJV
readings.orig: προνουμηνιων] και νουμηνιων Bᵃᵇ(ᵐᵍ) (inter προ et νουμ. ins νουμηνιων κ) ℵ
readings.en: the eves of new moons and new moons
readings.plain: the days before the new moons and the new moons

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: and the eves of new moons
readings.plain: the days before the new moons

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from Vaticanus. The list pairs each holy day with its eve ("the days before the Sabbaths and the Sabbaths"), and the new moons were feast days on which no one fasted (Mishnah Ta'anit 2:10). B's first scribe seems to have dropped the second word because it looks so like the first (προνουμηνιῶν, νουμηνιῶν). A corrector of B restored it in the margin.

a: called Chabris and Charmis
p: The KJV adds Uzziah to the elders Judith sends for; no Greek manuscript in Swete does.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (A spells the names Chabrim and Charmin); Vulgate (its 8:9)
readings.en: she called Chabris and Charmis
readings.plain: called Chabris and Charmis

readings.w: KJV (1611), from the Greek editions of its day
readings.en: to call Ozias and Chabris and Charmis
readings.plain: called Uzziah, Chabris and Charmis

why: All the Greek manuscripts in Swete and the Vulgate ("ad presbyteros Chabri et Charmi", Vulgate 8:9) name only two. Uzziah is added in some later Greek manuscripts (not in B, ℵ or A), which the KJV follows; the addition fits 8:28, where Uzziah answers her. Modern versions differ over printing it.

a: to shelter us on any days he wants
p: Alexandrinus has "and all" in place of "to shelter", which the KJV follows.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus
readings.en: to shelter (us) on whatever days he wishes
readings.plain: to shelter us on any days he wants

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), in Swete's notes; KJV
readings.orig: 15 σκεπασοι] και πασαις A [sic, for σκεπασαι]
readings.en: on whatever days he wishes, even on all days
readings.plain: to help us on whatever days he wants, even every day

why: The Plain English Translation follows Vaticanus. Alexandrinus' "and all" (καὶ πάσαις) looks like a misreading of σκεπάσαι; the KJV's "to defend us when he will, even every day" combines both.

a: he will demand our blood for its desecration
p: Sinaiticus names "the Lord" as the one who requires it; the KJV says "at our mouth".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ζητήσει τὴν βεβήλωσιν αὐτῶν ἐκ τοῦ αἵματος ἡμῶν
readings.en: he will seek their profanation from our blood
readings.plain: he will demand our blood for its desecration

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), in Swete's notes
readings.en: the Lord will require ...
readings.plain: the Lord will demand our blood for its desecration

readings.en: he will require the profanation thereof at our mouth
readings.plain: he will require its desecration from our mouth

why: The Plain English Translation follows Vaticanus; the subject is clearly God either way. Sinaiticus makes it explicit. The KJV's "at our mouth" has no support in Swete's manuscripts; it may come from a Greek edition that read "mouth" for "blood".

a: who violated a virgin's womb to defile her
p: The Greek says Shechem "loosed a virgin's womb". The KJV's "loosened the girdle" reads a different word, one letter apart.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete (corrected); Sinaiticus; Alexandrinus
readings.orig: οἳ ἔλυσαν μήτραν παρθένου εἰς μίασμα
readings.en: who loosed the womb of a virgin for defilement
readings.plain: who violated a virgin's womb to defile her

readings.en: who loosened the girdle of a maid to defile her
readings.plain: who loosened a virgin's belt to defile her

why: All of Swete's manuscripts read μήτραν, "womb", as again later in the verse. The KJV's "girdle" reflects μίτραν, a belt or headband, which differs by one vowel and gives an easier picture; it may be a scribe's or editor's correction, but many modern scholars and versions prefer μίτραν as the original, since "womb" twice in one verse is awkward. The first scribe of Vaticanus copied "a virgin's womb for defilement" twice, after "stripped" as well; a later hand marked the repeat.

a: Make my words and my deceit
p: Sinaiticus has "give me" for "my".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Alexandrinus; KJV
readings.en: give my word and deceit
readings.plain: Make my words and my deceit

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), in Swete's notes
readings.en: give me a word and deceit
readings.plain: Give me words and deceit to

why: The Plain English Translation follows Vaticanus. Sinaiticus' μοι, "to me", differs by one letter. Either way Judith asks God to bless her deceit.

a: Give your whole nation and every tribe the knowledge
p: Alexandrinus has "every nation", which the KJV follows.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus
readings.orig: ἐπὶ πᾶν τὸ ἔθνος σου καὶ πάσης φυλῆς ἐπίγνωσιν
readings.en: on all your nation and of every tribe knowledge
readings.plain: Give your whole nation and every tribe the knowledge

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), in Swete's notes; KJV
readings.orig: 14 παν το εθνος] παντος εθνους A
readings.en: of every nation
readings.plain: Give every nation and every tribe the knowledge

why: The Plain English Translation follows Vaticanus, where Judith prays that Israel will know God's power. Alexandrinus widens it to all nations, which fits the book's theme that the nations learn who is God (compare 14:10).

a: to catch the eye of any man who might see her
p: Vaticanus says she dressed "for the meeting" of men's eyes; Alexandrinus and a corrector of Sinaiticus say "for the deceiving".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: for the meeting of the eyes of men
readings.plain: to catch the eye of any man who might see her

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), in Swete's notes; a corrector of Sinaiticus
readings.en: for the deceiving of the eyes of men
readings.plain: to deceive the eyes of any man who might see her

readings.en: to allure the eyes of all men that should see her
readings.plain: to lure the eyes of any man who might see her

why: The Plain English Translation follows Vaticanus. The two Greek words differ by one letter (ἀπάντησιν, ἀπάτησιν). "Deceiving" matches the book's repeated word for Judith's plan (9:10, 13; 16:8), and some scholars prefer it for that reason; but a scribe could as easily have made it agree. The KJV's "allure" reads either way.

a: She bowed down to God,
p: Vaticanus has "she bowed down"; the KJV has "they worshipped".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus; Alexandrinus
readings.en: and she worshiped God
readings.plain: She bowed down to God,

readings.en: Then they worshipped God.
readings.plain: They bowed down to God.

why: All of Swete's manuscripts have the singular, and Judith goes on speaking in 10:9. The KJV's plural, not found in Swete's notes, makes the elders worship along with her.

a: as they had said.
t: As they said or as she said?
p: Vaticanus says the young men opened the gate "as they had said"; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and the KJV say "as she had said".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: as they had spoken
readings.plain: as they had said.

readings.w: Codices Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (ℵ A), in Swete's notes; KJV
readings.en: as she had spoken
readings.plain: as she had said.

why: The Plain English Translation follows Vaticanus: the elders give the order they had agreed to (8:35). The singular, "as she had spoken", makes Judith the one in command, and differs by one letter.

a: before he has done by my hand what he has planned
p: Alexandrinus and the KJV name "the Lord" as the one who will act.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἕως ἂν ποιήσῃ ἐν χειρί μου ἃ ἐβουλεύσατο
readings.en: until he does by my hand what he planned
readings.plain: before he has done by my hand what he has planned

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), in Swete's notes; KJV
readings.en: until the Lord does by my hand what he planned
readings.plain: before the Lord has done by my hand what he has planned

why: The Plain English Translation follows Vaticanus, where "he" is left open: Holofernes hears himself, the reader hears God. Alexandrinus spells out the meaning. (Sinaiticus is lost here.)

a: the children of his people
p: The Greek has "his people", God's people; the KJV has "her people".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Alexandrinus
readings.en: of the sons of his people
readings.plain: the children of his people

readings.en: of the children of her people
readings.plain: the children of her people

why: Swete's manuscripts read αὐτοῦ, "his", referring to "the Lord God of Israel". The KJV's "her" is not in Swete's notes; it may be a correction or a free rendering.

a: as they always did.
p: Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus add that the two women went out "to pray", as the KJV does.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete

readings.plain: as they always did.

readings.orig: 10 ουτων] + επι την προσευχην ℵΑ [sic, for αυτων]
readings.en: according to their custom, for prayer
readings.plain: as they always did, to pray.

why: The Plain English Translation follows Vaticanus. The longer text spells out what their custom was (12:6–8; 13:3).

a: in Israel
p: The KJV has "in Jerusalem".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Alexandrinus; Sinaiticus
readings.en: in Israel
readings.plain: in Israel

readings.en: in Jerusalem
readings.plain: in Jerusalem

why: All of Swete's manuscripts read "Israel". The KJV's "Jerusalem" is not in Swete's notes.

a: who led you to wound the head of our enemies' chief
p: Swete prints the reading of Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus here, not Vaticanus. The difference is one ending.

readings.w: Codices Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (ℵ A), in Swete's notes, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: εἰς τραῦμα κεφαλῆς ἄρχοντος ἐχθρῶν ἡμῶν
readings.en: to a wound of the head of the ruler of our enemies
readings.plain: who led you to wound the head of our enemies' chief

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), in Swete's notes
readings.en: to a wound, to the head of the ruler of our enemies
readings.plain: who guided you to strike at the head of our enemies' chief

readings.en: to the cutting off of the head of the chief of our enemies
readings.plain: who guided you to cut off the head of our enemies' chief

why: This is one of the few places where Swete departs from Vaticanus. B's accusative κεφαλήν makes "head" the goal of the movement, ℵA's genitive κεφαλῆς makes it part of the phrase "wound of the head". The sense is the same; the Plain English Translation follows Swete's text. Alexandrinus also reads "Blessed are you" with a verb, and "blessed" in a different form.

a: Betomasthaim, Choba and Chola
p: The place names differ in each manuscript.

p: Vaticanus prays that God "may be pleased"; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and the KJV say he "was pleased".

readings.plain: and may God be pleased with them

a: Sing to the Lord with cymbals!
p: Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus, followed by the KJV, have "my" here.

readings.plain: Sing to my Lord with cymbals!

a: Tune a psalm and a song of praise to him!
p: Alexandrinus reads "a new psalm" for "a psalm and praise"; the KJV and the Vulgate agree.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus
readings.en: tune to him a psalm and praise
readings.plain: Tune a psalm and a song of praise to him!

why: The Plain English Translation follows Vaticanus. The two readings differ only in how the same letters are divided: ΚΑΙΑΙΝΟΝ can be read as καὶ αἶνον, "and praise", or καινόν, "new". The "new song" of 16:13 may have helped the second reading.

a: set my mountains on fire
p: Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read "borders", as the KJV does.

why: The Plain English Translation follows Vaticanus. The two words, ὄρη and ὅρια, are very alike. In 2:10 Nebuchadnezzar orders the seizure of "all their territory" (πᾶν ὅριον αὐτῶν).

a: as a dedicated offering
p: Some manuscripts spell the word anathema, which can mean a thing devoted to destruction.

readings.plain: as a thing devoted

why: The Plain English Translation follows Vaticanus. In later Greek the two spellings were often confused, and here both mean a gift to God; ℵA also have "to the Lord" for "to God".

p: Vaticanus ends the book with "Amen". Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus do not.

a: which was ashamed of their deceit
p: The first hand of Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus lack "their deceit".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; a corrector of Sinaiticus
readings.en: which was ashamed of their deceit
readings.plain: which was ashamed of their deceit

readings.orig: om απατην ℵ* ᵛⁱᵈ (hab απατη ℵ¹) A

why: The Plain English Translation follows Vaticanus. Without the word, the line loses its play on deceit (the men who deceived are deceived), which is a theme of the whole book (9:10, 13; 12:16; 16:8). A scribe may have dropped it because the next word, ἀπατηθεῖσαν, begins the same way.

a: I will sing a new song to my God
p: Alexandrinus and the KJV have "to the Lord".
